prompt: Which storage account setting must be enabled to force all connections to use HTTPS instead of plaintext HTTP?
choices: Secure transfer required
Minimum TLS version 1.2
Allow Blob public access
Allow Shared Key authorization
correctAnswers: Secure transfer required
explanation: Secure transfer required rejects plaintext HTTP outright, so the connection never reaches the blob service unencrypted. Minimum TLS version is the closest miss and is a second, narrower control: it only matters once HTTPS is already in use, deciding which protocol versions are acceptable rather than whether encryption happens at all.

prompt: Which storage account setting enforces a minimum protocol version for encryption in transit?
choices: Minimum TLS version
Secure transfer required
Cross-tenant replication
Allow Blob public access
correctAnswers: Minimum TLS version
explanation: Minimum TLS version retires the deprecated protocol versions a client might negotiate, such as TLS 1.0 and 1.1. Secure transfer required is the tempting answer because it is the better-known encryption-in-transit setting, whereas it only forces HTTPS in general and leaves a client free to negotiate a weak version of it.

prompt: What does disabling 'Allow Blob public access' at the account level do?
choices: Prevents any container from ever being configured for anonymous public read access
Encrypts the account’s blobs at rest with a customer-managed key
Forces Microsoft Entra authentication for every single request made against the account
Blocks all inbound network traffic to the account from the internet
correctAnswers: Prevents any container from ever being configured for anonymous public read access
explanation: The account-level toggle overrides any container that is set, or later set, to anonymous public read — which is why it is the durable control rather than auditing containers one by one. Forcing Entra authentication for every request is the tempting over-reading: shared-key and SAS callers are unaffected by this setting, and disabling shared-key access is what governs them.

prompt: Which setting should be disabled to prevent clients from authenticating with the storage account's master access key?
choices: Allow Shared Key authorization
Allow blob anonymous access
Secure transfer required (HTTPS only)
Allow cross-tenant replication
correctAnswers: Allow Shared Key authorization
explanation: Disabling Allow Shared Key authorization removes the master key as an authentication path and therefore invalidates every account-key-signed SAS with it. Allow blob anonymous access is the closest miss and governs unauthenticated public readers, a different population entirely: it leaves the account key working for anyone who holds it.

prompt: Why is the storage account key considered a high-risk credential if leaked?
choices: It grants full, unscoped access to every service in the account, with no built-in expiry
It only ever grants read access to blobs, never write or delete
It rotates automatically every twenty-four hours, which limits how long a leaked copy stays usable
It cannot be used from anywhere outside the Azure portal at all
correctAnswers: It grants full, unscoped access to every service in the account, with no built-in expiry
explanation: The account key is a master credential — unlike a SAS, it isn't scoped or time-limited, so a leak exposes the entire account until the key is manually rotated.

prompt: Drag each shared access signature type onto the description that identifies it. Not every entry in the pool is used.

targets.label: Signed with the storage account key, and able to span several services and account-level operations
Signed with the storage account key, but scoped to a single service such as Blob
Signed with the caller's Microsoft Entra credentials, and revocable without rotating the account key
Not a signature at all: a server-side container object that a signature can reference for its permissions and expiry

explanation: Two questions separate the three signature types: what signs it, and how wide its scope is. The account key signs both the account and service SAS, which is why neither can be revoked without rotating that key — only the user delegation SAS is identity-backed. The stored access policy is included because candidates routinely list it as a fourth SAS type; it is the server-side object a signature points at, which is what makes central revocation possible in the first place.

prompt: What distinguishes an account SAS from a service SAS?
choices: An account SAS can span multiple services and grant account-level operations; a service SAS is scoped to one service
An account SAS is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials, whereas a service SAS is signed with the storage account key
An account SAS cannot be given an expiry time, unlike a service SAS which always carries one
A service SAS never requires a defined resource scope, so it always covers the whole account
correctAnswers: An account SAS can span multiple services and grant account-level operations; a service SAS is scoped to one service
explanation: Both account and service SAS are signed with the account key — the difference is breadth of scope, not the signing credential.

prompt: Why is a user delegation SAS considered more secure than an account or service SAS?
choices: Revoking it doesn't require rotating the account key — it can be revoked via Entra permission changes or delegation key expiry
It never expires, which makes it considerably simpler to manage across many client applications
It grants access to every container in the account instead of only to a single named one
It is stored inside the storage account rather than being shared with the client, so the client never holds a copy of the token
correctAnswers: Revoking it doesn't require rotating the account key — it can be revoked via Entra permission changes or delegation key expiry
explanation: Because it isn't signed with the account key, revoking access doesn't require the disruptive step of rotating the key and breaking every other SAS issued from it.

prompt: What is the purpose of a stored access policy on a container?
choices: It attaches server-side constraints (permissions, expiry) to SAS tokens so they can be revoked or changed centrally without reissuing them
It encrypts the container's blobs at rest with a customer-managed key held in Azure Key Vault
It restricts network access to that container to a specific set of named virtual network subnets
It forces HTTPS on every request made to that container, and rejects any plaintext HTTP attempt before it can reach the blob service at all
correctAnswers: It attaches server-side constraints (permissions, expiry) to SAS tokens so they can be revoked or changed centrally without reissuing them
explanation: A stored access policy holds the permissions and expiry server-side, so editing or deleting it changes or revokes every SAS bound to it at once — without rotating the account key and without reissuing tokens. That is the point worth remembering: a SAS with no stored access policy cannot be revoked individually at all, and the only remedy left is a key rotation that breaks every other token too.

prompt: A team needs to be able to instantly revoke a leaked SAS token without invalidating other SAS tokens issued from the same account key. What should they have used?
choices: A SAS linked to a stored access policy, so only that policy needs to change
Rotating both of the storage account access keys at once
Disabling Allow Blob public access across the whole account
Disabling the storage account entirely until the leaked token has expired on its own
correctAnswers: A SAS linked to a stored access policy, so only that policy needs to change
explanation: Rotating the account key would invalidate every SAS signed with it, not just the leaked one. A stored access policy allows surgical revocation.

prompt: For each statement about revoking shared access signatures, select Yes if it is true.

statements.text: Rotating a storage account key immediately invalidates every account and service SAS signed with it.
A SAS with no stored access policy can be revoked individually, without affecting others.
Editing a stored access policy changes or revokes every SAS bound to that policy at once.
A user delegation SAS can be revoked through Entra permissions, without rotating the key.

explanation: Revocability is decided at issue time, not at incident time — which is the practical lesson. A key-signed SAS with no stored access policy can only be revoked by rotating the key, and that invalidates every other token signed with it; the second statement is the assumption that makes a leak far more disruptive than expected. A stored access policy or a user delegation SAS both give you a revocation path that does not take everything else down with it.

prompt: What is the effect of a service endpoint on a storage account's network exposure?
choices: Traffic stays on the Azure backbone and the storage firewall can trust a specific subnet, but the account keeps a public IP
The account is assigned a private IP address inside the virtual network, so its public endpoint is removed from DNS entirely
All internet access to the account is blocked, including requests originating in other Azure regions
It encrypts traffic between the virtual network and the storage account from end to end
correctAnswers: Traffic stays on the Azure backbone and the storage firewall can trust a specific subnet, but the account keeps a public IP
explanation: A service endpoint extends the VNet's identity to the storage firewall so a specific subnet can be trusted, and keeps traffic on the Azure backbone — but the account keeps its public IP and stays publicly addressable. Believing it removes the public endpoint is the misconception that leads teams to report zero internet exposure when the endpoint still answers; that is what a private endpoint does.

prompt: What is the effect of adding a private endpoint to a storage account?
choices: The account receives a private IP address inside the VNet, and traffic never touches the public endpoint
The account's public IP address is merely restricted to a single named subnet
It only affects control-plane management calls to the account and leaves data-plane access on the public endpoint
It requires Shared Key authorization to be left enabled on the storage account
correctAnswers: The account receives a private IP address inside the VNet, and traffic never touches the public endpoint
explanation: A private endpoint attaches a NIC with a private VNet IP to the storage account's data plane. Restricting a public IP by subnet describes a service endpoint instead.

prompt: A requirement states a backup storage account must have zero public internet exposure and be reachable only from an on-premises network over ExpressRoute. Which network configuration meets this?
choices: Public network access Disabled, with a private endpoint in a VNet reachable over ExpressRoute
Selected networks, with a service endpoint applied to the ExpressRoute gateway subnet
Enabled from all networks, with an IP restriction rule allow-listing only the on-premises public IP range
Allow trusted Microsoft services only, with every other network blocked
correctAnswers: Public network access Disabled, with a private endpoint in a VNet reachable over ExpressRoute
explanation: Only Disabled plus a private endpoint removes the public endpoint entirely while remaining reachable over ExpressRoute. The IP allow-list is the tempting alternative because access does become restricted, whereas the endpoint stays public and publicly resolvable — it narrows who may connect rather than removing the exposure the requirement names.

prompt: Four descriptions of what a storage network control actually does. Assign the control for each; two entries in the list describe none of them.
sources: Public network access enabled from all networks

targets.label: The account keeps a public IP, restricted to named subnets, over the Azure backbone
The account gets a private IP in the VNet, so the public endpoint can be removed
Any client on the internet may connect, with authentication the only barrier left
targets.correctSource: Public network access enabled from all networks

targets.label: A named first-party Azure service bypasses the firewall for a legitimate integration

explanation: The first two are the pair that decides whether "no public exposure" is a true statement: a service endpoint leaves the address publicly resolvable and merely restricts who may use it, whereas a private endpoint replaces it. The third is the least secure of the three postures — and worth contrasting with an empty Selected networks, which looks unfinished and is actually closed. The two unused entries govern traffic between resources and the terms of a SAS.

prompt: What does Microsoft Defender for Storage's malware scanning check?
choices: Uploaded blobs, using Microsoft Defender Antivirus, at ingestion time
Existing NSG rules on the subnet from which the storage account is reached
TLS certificate validity on any mapped custom domains
SAS token expiry dates across all of the account's containers
correctAnswers: Uploaded blobs, using Microsoft Defender Antivirus, at ingestion time
explanation: Malware scanning inspects blob CONTENT at upload time using Microsoft Defender Antivirus, which is why it is a data-plane control rather than a configuration check. The NSG, certificate and SAS-expiry options are tempting because each is a real thing worth reviewing, whereas none of them looks inside a blob and none is part of this feature.

prompt: Besides malware scanning, what else does Microsoft Defender for Storage detect?
choices: Anomalous access patterns and sensitive-data exfiltration threats
Missing resource tags on the account's containers
Expired TLS certificates on custom domains mapped to the storage account
Orphaned SAS tokens left valid after their task finished
correctAnswers: Anomalous access patterns and sensitive-data exfiltration threats
explanation: Beyond malware, Defender for Storage detects anomalous access patterns and the exfiltration of data classified as sensitive — behavioural signals rather than static findings. The three distractors are hygiene checks that a policy or a script would catch: missing tags, expired certificates and stale SAS tokens are not threats detected at access time.

prompt: At what scope can Microsoft Defender for Storage be enabled?
choices: Per subscription or per individual storage account
Only per management group, inherited downward
Only per individual storage account, never per subscription
Only globally, for every subscription in the tenant
correctAnswers: Per subscription or per individual storage account
explanation: Defender for Storage is enabled per subscription for broad coverage, or per storage account when only some need it — the two scopes together are what allow a cost and coverage trade-off. Reading it as account-only or as tenant-wide is the misconception, and neither restriction exists: each one would remove exactly the flexibility that makes the plan affordable to switch on.

prompt: For each statement about encryption at rest on an Azure storage account, select Yes if it is true.

statements.text: Storage Service Encryption is always on and cannot be turned off.
Infrastructure encryption adds a second encryption layer, with a separate key.
Infrastructure encryption can be enabled on an existing account at any time.
A customer-managed key changes whose key is used, not whether encryption happens.

explanation: Three layers stack and none of them is a substitute for another: SSE is unconditional, a CMK only changes key ownership, and infrastructure encryption adds a second pass for defence in depth. The third statement is the one with an operational consequence — infrastructure encryption is a creation-time choice rather than a toggle, so an account that needs it later has to be recreated and its data copied across.

prompt: When is a customer-managed key (CMK) for storage encryption most useful?
choices: When the organization needs to control the encryption key's lifecycle (rotation, revocation) themselves via Key Vault
When Shared Key authorization must remain enabled because legacy client tooling cannot authenticate with Microsoft Entra identities
When anonymous public blob access is required in order to serve a static website from the account
When TLS 1.0 must still be supported for legacy clients that connect to the account
correctAnswers: When the organization needs to control the encryption key's lifecycle (rotation, revocation) themselves via Key Vault
explanation: A customer-managed key moves the key's lifecycle — rotation, revocation, and the ability to make data unreadable by destroying it — into a Key Vault the organization controls. The distractors are all tempting because each is a legitimate storage requirement, whereas none of them is met by CMK: shared-key access, anonymous access and TLS floor are independent settings that a CMK never touches.

prompt: Is Storage Service Encryption (SSE) at rest optional on an Azure storage account?
choices: No, it is always enabled and cannot be turned off
Yes, it has to be enabled manually on each container
Yes, but only for Premium storage accounts
No, it only applies to Table storage
correctAnswers: No, it is always enabled and cannot be turned off
explanation: Storage Service Encryption is always on, for every account and every service, and cannot be turned off — so there is nothing to enable and nothing to forget. The Premium-only and Table-only options are tempting because Azure does have tier-dependent features, whereas encryption at rest is not one of them; the optional layer is infrastructure encryption, which adds a second pass on top.

prompt: A document storage account must reject anonymous container access and plaintext HTTP, and must never rely on the master key. Complete the three settings.

options: Public network access = Enabled from all networks

explanation: Each clause of the requirement maps to exactly one setting, and none of the three is redundant — dropping any one leaves its clause unmet. The third blank has the widest consequence: disabling shared-key access also invalidates every account-key-signed SAS, because those tokens are signed with the key being refused, so Entra with RBAC becomes the only way in rather than merely the preferred one.

prompt: Which authentication model should replace Shared Key access for a storage account under a 'no master key usage' requirement?
choices: Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC role assignments
A single shared connection string distributed to all apps
Anonymous container access scoped to read-only
A service endpoint with IP allow-listing
correctAnswers: Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC role assignments
explanation: Entra ID + RBAC lets each identity get scoped, revocable, auditable permissions instead of a single all-powerful key. A shared connection string and anonymous access both reintroduce the risks the requirement is meant to eliminate.

prompt: What is the purpose of the 'Allow trusted Microsoft services to access this storage account' exception on the storage firewall?
choices: To let specific first-party Azure services bypass network restrictions for legitimate integration scenarios
To allow any authenticated Microsoft Entra user through the storage firewall regardless of their network location
To permit Shared Key authorization, but only for Microsoft support engineers
To disable minimum-TLS version enforcement for Microsoft-owned IP ranges
correctAnswers: To let specific first-party Azure services bypass network restrictions for legitimate integration scenarios
explanation: This exception is scoped to a curated list of Microsoft services (e.g. certain resource providers in the same tenant) needing legitimate access, not a blanket bypass for any user or purpose.

prompt: Which Azure CLI command sets `--allow-shared-key-access false` and `--allow-blob-public-access false` when provisioning a storage account?
choices: az storage account create
az storage account keys renew
az storage container create
az role assignment create
correctAnswers: az storage account create
explanation: These are account-level properties set at creation (or update) time via `az storage account create`/`update`. The other commands manage keys, containers, or RBAC assignments respectively, not these account-wide toggles.

prompt: Which PowerShell cmdlet updates a storage account's minimum TLS version and Shared Key access setting?
choices: Set-AzStorageAccount
Set-AzStorageBlobContent
New-AzStorageContext
Set-AzStorageContainerAcl
correctAnswers: Set-AzStorageAccount
explanation: Set-AzStorageAccount manages account-level properties, MinimumTlsVersion and AllowSharedKeyAccess among them. Set-AzStorageContainerAcl is the closest miss and operates one level down, on a container's public-access level, so it cannot reach an account-wide setting. The other two write blob content and build a context object.

prompt: Complete the Azure CLI command so that it issues a user delegation SAS — one signed with the caller's Microsoft Entra identity rather than with the storage account key.
template: az storage container generate-sas --account-name scanned --name docs --permissions r --expiry 2026-08-10 [[b1]] [[b2]]
explanation: Both parameters are needed and neither works alone: `--auth-mode login` tells the CLI to authenticate as the signed-in principal, and `--as-user` is what makes the resulting token a user delegation SAS rather than one signed with the account key. `--auth-mode key` is the tempting choice because it is the default, and it is exactly what produces an account-key-signed token that cannot be revoked without rotating the key. This is tested as a fill-in rather than as a choice between whole command lines, because only the two parameters carry the knowledge — and a correct command line is always the longest option, which gives the answer away.

prompt: Which two settings should be disabled to reduce a storage account's attack surface? (Choose two.)
choices: Allow Blob public access
Allow Shared Key authorization
Secure transfer required (HTTPS)
Infrastructure encryption at rest
correctAnswers: Allow Blob public access
Allow Shared Key authorization
explanation: Blob public access and Shared Key authorization are the two toggles that should be turned OFF for hardening. Secure transfer required and infrastructure encryption should instead be turned ON.

prompt: Which two statements about a user delegation SAS are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: It is signed with the caller's Microsoft Entra credentials
It is signed with one of the two storage account keys rather than with a user's identity
It can be revoked via Entra role/permission changes without rotating the account key
It cannot be scoped down to a single named blob container
correctAnswers: It is signed with the caller's Microsoft Entra credentials
It can be revoked via Entra role/permission changes without rotating the account key
explanation: A user delegation SAS is the Entra-signed alternative to account/service SAS, which is why revoking it doesn't require the disruptive step of rotating the account key.

prompt: Which two capabilities does Microsoft Defender for Storage provide? (Choose two.)
choices: Malware scanning on blob upload
Automatic account key rotation on a schedule
TLS certificate issuance for custom domains
Sensitive-data exfiltration alerts
correctAnswers: Malware scanning on blob upload
Sensitive-data exfiltration alerts
explanation: Defender for Storage detects threats — malware on upload and exfiltration of sensitive data. It does not manage key rotation or issue certificates.

prompt: Referring to requirement 1 (the scanned-documents storage account must reject anonymous container access and plaintext HTTP, and must never authorize access with the account's master key), which combination of settings is correct?
choices: Allow Blob public access = Disabled, Secure transfer required = Enabled, Allow Shared Key authorization = Disabled
Allow Blob public access = Enabled with container-level private access, Minimum TLS = 1.0, Allow Shared Key authorization = Disabled
Allow Shared Key authorization = Enabled, restricted to the read-only secondary key
Public network access = Disabled, but Allow Shared Key authorization = Enabled for clients
correctAnswers: Allow Blob public access = Disabled, Secure transfer required = Enabled, Allow Shared Key authorization = Disabled
explanation: All three requirements map to account-level toggles being set correctly together. Leaving Shared Key authorization enabled — even 'restricted to read-only keys,' which isn't a real capability — would still allow master-key authentication.

prompt: Requirement 1 also implies clients must authenticate without the account key. Which approach grants a third-party scanning vendor scoped, time-limited access to a single container without ever sharing the account key?
choices: A user delegation SAS scoped to the specific container with a short expiry
An account SAS signed with the storage account key
Sharing the account's primary key over a secure channel
Enabling anonymous container read access, restricted to the vendor's IP range
correctAnswers: A user delegation SAS scoped to the specific container with a short expiry
explanation: A user delegation SAS is signed with the caller's Entra credentials, so it is scoped, time-limited, and revocable without the account key ever existing in the transaction. An account SAS is the trap: it looks equally scoped and equally short-lived, whereas it is signed with the very key the requirement forbids — and disabling shared-key access would invalidate it outright.

prompt: Referring to requirement 2 (the backup archive storage account must be reachable only from a specific on-premises network via ExpressRoute, with zero internet exposure), which network configuration is correct?
choices: Public network access Disabled, with a private endpoint in a VNet reachable over ExpressRoute
Selected networks, with only the on-premises public IP range allow-listed
Enabled from all networks, with Secure transfer required left enabled
A service endpoint on the ExpressRoute gateway subnet, with public network access left Enabled on the account
correctAnswers: Public network access Disabled, with a private endpoint in a VNet reachable over ExpressRoute
explanation: Only Disabled plus a private endpoint removes the public endpoint, which is what "zero internet exposure" requires. Allow-listing the on-premises public IP range is the tempting alternative and leaves a publicly reachable endpoint that merely refuses most callers; a service endpoint with public access left Enabled fails for the same reason.

prompt: Proposed solution: Set every container's individual access level to Private, but leave Allow Blob public access enabled at the account level, and keep Allow Shared Key authorization enabled for app compatibility. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Leaving Allow Shared Key authorization enabled still permits master-key authentication, and leaving Allow Blob public access enabled at the account risks a future container being flipped to anonymous — neither goal condition is guaranteed.

prompt: Proposed solution: Disable Allow Blob public access and Allow Shared Key authorization at the account level, and require every client to authenticate via Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC role assignments. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: Disabling both account-level toggles closes the anonymous path and the master-key path together, and Entra ID with Azure RBAC supplies the scoped replacement — so access is redirected rather than simply removed. Note the prerequisite this accepts: any client that cannot authenticate with an Entra identity stops working immediately, which is the migration cost the requirement is choosing to pay.

prompt: Proposed solution: Keep Allow Blob public access and Allow Shared Key authorization at their default (enabled) values, but rotate the storage account key every 24 hours. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Rotating the key doesn't prevent anonymous access, nor does it stop key-based authentication from being used between rotations — it only limits, rather than eliminates, the exposure window.

prompt: Order the steps to issue a revocable, container-scoped SAS token backed by a stored access policy.
reorderItems: Create the stored access policy on the container (permissions, start/expiry)
Generate a SAS token that references the stored access policy
Distribute the SAS token to the client
Revoke or modify access at any time by updating or deleting the stored access policy
explanation: The policy must exist before a SAS can reference it; the token is then distributed and used, and later governed centrally by editing the same policy rather than reissuing tokens.

prompt: Build the sequence that moves a storage account from open network access to a fully private posture. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Create a private endpoint for the storage account in the target VNet subnet
Create and link the privatelink private DNS zone so the FQDN resolves privately
Verify connectivity to the account over the private IP from inside the VNet
Set the account's public network access to Disabled
Set the account's public network access to Disabled before anything else
Add an IP rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 so nothing breaks during the migration
Disable soft delete on the account to simplify the cutover
correctOrder: Create a private endpoint for the storage account in the target VNet subnet
Create and link the privatelink private DNS zone so the FQDN resolves privately
Verify connectivity to the account over the private IP from inside the VNet
Set the account's public network access to Disabled
explanation: The private path has to exist, resolve and be PROVEN before the public one is removed — the verification step is what separates a migration from a hope. Disabling public access first is the excluded action that causes an outage, allowing 0.0.0.0/0 is the opposite mistake and grants exactly the exposure being removed, and disabling soft delete has no bearing on networking, whereas it does remove your ability to recover from a mistake.

prompt: Configure this simplified storage account security screen so the account rejects anonymous access, requires HTTPS with a modern TLS version, and never accepts the account's master key.
explanation: Secure transfer On rejects HTTP, TLS 1.2 retires the deprecated versions, and disabling both Blob public access and account key access removes the anonymous and master-key routes — leaving Entra ID with RBAC as the only way in. The trap is treating the TLS field as sufficient on its own: at TLS 1.0 or 1.1 the connection is still encrypted, which is why a reviewer can pass over it.

prompt: A single named Microsoft Foundry resource must be allowed through a storage account's network firewall, without opening the account to an entire virtual network or to the public internet. Which mechanism is designed for this?
choices: A resource instance rule scoped to the Foundry resource's ID
The Allow trusted Microsoft services exception
A service endpoint applied to every subnet in the virtual network
Disabling the storage account firewall entirely
correctAnswers: A resource instance rule scoped to the Foundry resource's ID
explanation: A resource instance rule allows one named resource, by its resource ID, through the firewall. Allow trusted Microsoft services is the tempting neighbour and is far broader: it admits an entire class of first-party services rather than the one resource, so it grants access to instances nobody reviewed.

prompt: What is the key difference between a storage account resource instance rule and the 'Allow trusted Microsoft services' exception?
choices: A resource instance rule scopes access to one named resource by ID; the trusted-services exception opens access to an entire class of first-party services
They are functionally identical and interchangeable, so either one can be used to reach exactly the same result
A resource instance rule only works while Shared Key authorization is left enabled on the storage account
The trusted-services exception is more restrictive than a resource instance rule, because it names individual first-party services rather than a whole class of them
correctAnswers: A resource instance rule scopes access to one named resource by ID; the trusted-services exception opens access to an entire class of first-party services
explanation: A resource instance rule is the narrower, more targeted option — it names a specific resource ID rather than trusting an entire category of Microsoft services.

prompt: A security review flags that a storage account has 'Allow trusted Microsoft services' enabled, but investigation shows only one specific Azure AI service resource actually needs access. What is the recommended remediation?
choices: Replace the broad exception with a resource instance rule scoped to that one AI service resource's ID
Enable Allow Blob public access instead, so the AI service needs no firewall exception
Re-enable Shared Key authorization so the AI service can authenticate with the account key
Leave the setting as it is, on the grounds that a resource instance rule and the trusted-services exception are equally secure
correctAnswers: Replace the broad exception with a resource instance rule scoped to that one AI service resource's ID
explanation: Once only one resource actually needs access, a resource instance rule scoped to its ID is strictly narrower than the blanket exception and is the recommended replacement. Leaving the setting alone on the grounds that the two are equally secure is the reasoning to reject: trusted services admits a whole service class, so the exception stays wider than the need it was added for rather than matching it.
